behaviors.summary: Master and PhD accounts are treated as students. Students and Professor can use the general observation tools.
conditions: Account roles come from the application’s configured memberships, not from what an agent says.
Recognizing a role does not by itself grant access to a particular job.

behaviors.summary: Only Professor can approve, reject, dispatch or administratively stop a job through these operations.
conditions: Approval requires a queued job, the current version and a resource request within the owner’s quota.
Rejection requires the current queued version and a rejection decision.
Dispatch also requires a valid approval, an eligible free node and the waiting-queue selection.
Stopping requires a reason parameter and an allowed state transition. Tool confirmation is separate.

behaviors.summary: Students can submit within quota, revise their own queued jobs, and cancel or send structured completion reports for their own jobs.
conditions: Revision checks the new resource request against the caller’s quota.
Cancellation requires a reason parameter and an allowed transition; the application validates the reason text.
A structured completion report checks the sender and job owner. Sending one does not mark the job completed.
Free-text messages are not covered by this completion-report check.

behaviors.summary: Master can request CPU up to 4 cores, 8 GB and 20 minutes. PhD can request CPU or GPU up to 8 cores, 32 GB and 60 minutes.
conditions: All limits must hold together. Stored jobs are checked against their owner’s quota.
These checks limit requested runtime. They do not stop a job after that many minutes.
Positive, well-formed resource values are an application-validation assumption.
behaviors.question: Should the system automatically stop a Master job if it runs longer than 20 minutes?

behaviors.summary: A node is usable only if it is free, matches the requested CPU or GPU type, and has enough cores and memory.
conditions: Availability comes from the current node record supplied by the application.
This condition alone does not authorize dispatch or reserve a node.

behaviors.summary: Students can read their own job records; Professor can read any stored job. Bulk and private views still rely on application filtering.
conditions: Single-job reads check the stored owner against the caller.
The private-owner relation includes the caller’s own records and Professor’s access to ordinary users’ records.
Allowing a bulk-view call does not itself filter its returned content.
These rules do not establish isolation across every message, model context or export.

behaviors.summary: An approval is current only when Professor approved the same task version and resource request under the current policy configuration.
conditions: The job must point to that approval record.
Task identity, version, task content, CPU/GPU type, cores, memory and requested minutes must match.
The approval’s policy configuration must also match the current configuration.
behaviors.question: If cluster policy changes after approval, should the job need another approval?

behaviors.summary: A job can be marked COMPLETED only with a simulator receipt confirming that its current run ended successfully.
conditions: The caller must be allowed to read the job, and the job must currently be RUNNING.
The chosen receipt must match the current job, run, task content, node and allocation generation.
Successful exit means the application recorded exit_code = 0. The original wording does not explicitly choose this definition of completion.
Receipt lineage must lead to the job owner. This relies on the application’s evidence mapping.
Only the configured Runner can record completion for an existing running job.
The runtime still requires an allowed state transition and no denial or invariant failure.
behaviors.question: A run has ended and has a simulator receipt, but it failed. Should it still be possible to mark the job COMPLETED?

behaviors.summary: A stored job state must occur in the configured lifecycle.
conditions: The configured states are QUEUED, RUNNING, COMPLETED and TERMINATED.
A state outside that set raises an invariant failure. This does not perform the business operation.

behaviors.summary: Running jobs and occupied nodes must agree on the current run, task version and allocation.
conditions: A running job needs a matching run and node allocation, with enough capacity for its request.
A node referring to a missing run, a mismatched job or a different node is inconsistent.
An inconsistency blocks a guarded operation. If discovered after a business effect, the current integration stops the session; it cannot undo that effect.

behaviors.summary: When dispatch is requested, eligible jobs compete for the same free node. PhD goes first until an eligible Master job has been skipped three times; equal priorities use submission order.
conditions: Candidates must be queued, have current approval and fit their owner’s quota.
Each candidate selects its first free compatible node in the application’s configured node order.
After three recorded skips, Master has higher priority than PhD.
Jobs selecting different nodes do not compete with one another.
This constrains dispatch decisions. It does not guarantee that a scheduler will eventually request dispatch.
behaviors.question: Should the system start waiting jobs by itself when the scheduler makes no dispatch requests?

P2.2: Single-job reads are checked, but other messages and model contexts are not fully mediated. A private peer message can still reach the wrong student.
The application needs checks on every relevant output channel before this requirement is fully supported.
P2.3: The application has no complete check of private contents in arbitrary messages or Professor replies.
A sender’s claim about where information came from is not sufficient evidence.
P2.4: The application returns UNAVAILABLE for both a missing job and a job the caller cannot read.
This depends on response handling, not only on deciding whether a read is allowed.
P2.5: The original application exposes quotas, node specifications and aggregate availability.
Timing and public availability can still reveal indirect information, as the policy allows.
P2.6: The evaluation trace contains information from multiple participants.
Keeping that trace away from student agents depends on deployment and export access; this review does not verify those channels.
P2.7: No complete credential detector or secret-flow protection is installed.
Prompt construction, logs and submitted files need their own verified controls.
P3.3: Only queued jobs can be revised. A successful revision increments the task version and clears the current approval.
The application must record the returned version and resource request so that old approvals no longer match.
P3.4: Approval records permission without starting the job or allocating a node.
This is behavior of the original approval operation; translating a rule does not implement it.
P4.1: The runtime checks allowed state changes, while the application performs the actual job and node operations.
Job, run and node records must stay synchronized.
P4.3: A successful submission creates a queued job. The runtime checks that initial state before saving its policy records.
P4.4: A queued job can start or terminate. A running job can complete or terminate.
Repeated stop requests for an already terminal job are acknowledged without restarting it.
The state update follows confirmation from the original operation.
P4.5: A rejected queued request or a successful queued cancellation ends in TERMINATED.
Rejecting a job is an allowed business operation, distinct from refusing permission to call a tool.
P4.9: Releasing a node follows the confirmation and current-run checks described in P6. This sentence adds no separate permission.
P6.1: The original application confirms completion or stopping and releases the current allocation.
Business records and policy records do not share a transaction. An uncertain update stops the session rather than claiming to undo the business effect.
P6.3: A failed stop keeps the running state and node allocation.
Only a confirmed stop permits the corresponding state and allocation updates.
P6.4: Before release, the original application compares both the run and allocation generation with the node’s current owner.
The policy records are updated from the confirmed result.
P6.5: Old or mismatched completion notifications must not affect a newer run.
Repeating a terminal stop returns an acknowledgement without releasing another allocation. These behaviors rely on application handling.
P6.6: This is an example of the current-run check: an old Master notification must leave a newer PhD allocation intact.
P6.7: Students may cancel their own jobs. Professor may request an administrative stop. The original operation must still confirm stopping.
